questions.prompt: Twenty-five students each took a random sample of size 60 and built a 95% confidence interval for p. The true value is p = 0.6. How many of the intervals capture p?
solutionSteps: An interval captures p when it crosses the vertical line at p = 0.6.

23/25 = 92% captured p. A 95% method captures p about 95% of the time in the long run, so we expect about 23.75 of 25 intervals to capture it; with only 25 intervals the count varies by chance. 23 is within the range chance usually gives (21 to 25 of 25), so the result is consistent with a 95% method.

questions.prompt: The figure shows a left-tailed test of H₀: μ = 20 at α = 0.05 when the true mean is 14. Which region’s area is the probability of a Type I error?
questions.answer: Region 1
solutionSteps: Region 1: H₀ is true but the sample lands beyond the critical value, so we wrongly reject (Type I error, area α).
Region 2: Hₐ is true but the sample does not land beyond the critical value, so we wrongly fail to reject (Type II error, area β).
Region 3: Hₐ is true and we correctly reject (power = 1 − β). So the probability of a Type I error is region 1.

questions.prompt: The figure shows a right-tailed test of H₀: μ = 100 at α = 0.01 when the true mean is 108. Which region’s area is the probability of a Type II error?
questions.answer: Region 2
solutionSteps: Region 1: H₀ is true but the sample lands beyond the critical value, so we wrongly reject (Type I error, area α).

questions.answer: about 0.27
solutionSteps: If the treatment has no effect, the successes would be split between groups at random; the dot plot shows the differences that happen by chance alone.
Count dots at or above 0.12: 27 of 100.
Estimated p-value ≈ 0.27. This is not very small, so chance alone could explain the difference.

questions.prompt: Free response (Beyond AP: Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Tests). A claim says the distribution of how students get to school is bus 30%, car 40%, walk 20%, bike 10%. A random sample of 200 gives bus 65, car 77, walk 34, bike 24. Test the claim at α = 0.05 (Beyond AP: chi-square goodness of fit).
questions.answer: (a) H₀: the claimed distribution is correct; Hₐ: it is not; (b) Chi-square GOF test; random; expected counts 60, 80, 40, 20 all ≥ 5; (c) χ² ≈ 2.23; df = 3; p-value ≈ 0.5262; (d) Fail to reject H₀: not convincing evidence against the claim

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Chi-square GOF test; random; expected counts 60, 80, 40, 20 all ≥ 5

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Do: find the chi-square statistic, df and p-value. Round χ² to two decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Conclude: state your conclusion in context, and justify it with the p-value.
parts.answer: Fail to reject H₀: not convincing evidence against the claim

solutionSteps: (a) H₀: p_bus = 0.3, p_car = 0.4, p_walk = 0.2, p_bike = 0.1. Hₐ: at least one proportion differs.

(b) Scoring, 1 point: Test and expected counts.
(c) Scoring, 2 points: 1 point χ²; 1 point df and p-value.
(d) 0.5262 > 0.05, so we fail to reject H₀ about how students get to school.

questions.prompt: Free response (Interpreting Confidence Levels and Checking Inference Conditions). A random sample of 300 from 50,000 voters in a state finds 167 who support a new park tax. A researcher builds a 90% confidence interval for the proportion.
questions.answer: (a) Random sample; 300 < 10% of 50,000; 167 and 133 are both ≥ 10; (b) If we took many random samples of 300 and built an interval from each, about 90% would capture the true proportion; (c) Wider, because it needs a larger critical value (z* = 2.576 vs 1.645); (d) Once computed, the interval either captures p or it does not; the 90% refers to the method
